cim_eredeti: 7 sure-fire ways to blow your AI budget
szoveg_eredeti:
CIOs have always felt pressure to deploy emerging technologies rapidly. Implementation brings challenges, including calculating and measuring upfront investment costs. Deploy too quickly, and when the hype fades, many IT departments are left with a costly architecture to support, security gaps, and operational issues.

The same trend is happening with AI. Many CIOs procured enterprise-wide AI model licenses and empowered employees to experiment with language models and develop AI agents. Others asked DevOps teams to accelerate AI code generation and vibe coding. The shift from rapid experimentation to deploying more AI capabilities to production can leave CIOs with mounting AI debt and AI FinOps gaps.

CIOs’ near-term concern is managing budgets amid consumption-based AI pricing models. Even as AI token costs decrease, more employees are using AI, and agents are given more challenging, expensive assignments. Here are seven common mistakes IT leaders make that result in blown AI budgets.

Most CIOs and CAIOs recognize the need to establish AI strategies focused on areas where AI can provide lasting business value. But many fail to quantify targeted business outcomes, leaving employees to use adoption metrics as the primary objective.

“Every token spent on a pilot that never proves its value is money leaders can’t get back and lost opportunity cost, which is a governance failure more than a technology one,” says Rob Scudiere, CTO at Verint. “Every agent and workflow should have to earn its budget by showing results that achieve the desired business outcome, or lose it.”

Kris Beevers, CEO and cofounder of Netbox Labs, says to use existing business metrics to see whether the areas adopting AI are improving them faster. “If adoption is climbing but the outcomes aren’t moving with it, that’s a pretty good signal to rethink where you’re spending,” Beevers says.

Recommendation: Financial impacts may be hard to target during experimental phases, but employees should set financial objectives before moving AI agents into development and deployment phases.

CIOs may find they have a real mess on their hands when a few pilot AI agents quickly scale to thousands running in production. Much of AI governance focuses on identifying owners, setting data-access rules, defining target business outcomes, and establishing accuracy guidelines. CIOs must also educate employees on underlying cost factors, including model selection and platform standardization.

“Delayed AI governance gets framed as a compliance risk, but it’s just as much a budgetary concern,” says Guy Bourgault, head of agentic systems at Concentrix. “The longer organizations wait to define ownership, standards, and controls, the more they end up funding inefficiency, rather than progress.”

Varun Goswami, global head of product and AI at Newgen, says AI budgets are wasted on scattered pilots, duplicated integrations, and agents that run quietly without ever proving value. “Build on one governed platform rather than a dozen parallel stacks, reuse templates and connectors instead of custom-building each use case, and match the model to the job rather than routing everything to the priciest foundation model,” Goswami recommends.

Data quality is a third concern, according to Collibra and The Harris Poll, with 96% of IT leaders saying project failure almost always traces back to poor data foundations, and 51% reporting significant staff hours spent manually correcting autonomous AI agent outputs. CIOs should set data quality metrics and establish data products to build a trustworthy AI context layer.

Recommendation: CIOs should update and communicate their AI governance policies monthly, as AI cost, capabilities, compliance, and security considerations evolve rapidly.

Much of the discussion around AI token economics, or tokenomics, focuses on the costs of using different AI models. But the FinOps Foundation defines tokenomics as “the study of how the production, distribution, and consumption of tokens generate business outcomes and AI value within an organization.”

Because many organizations use multiple models, SaaS with AI agents, and internally developed AI agents, CIOs should partner with the CFO to measure total impact, including AI’s direct token costs, employee efforts, ongoing inference costs, and the value delivered.

“Companies can quickly overspend on AI when they focus too narrowly on token consumption, and the starting point should always be the business outcome,” says Prakash Kota, CIO at UKG. “I use the Three T’s: does the work require talent for judgment or expertise, can existing tools solve it efficiently, or do tokens create enough value to justify the investment?”

CIOs should then set AI budgets at the employee, department, and workflow levels. Each group’s budget should be reviewed and adjusted regularly based on outcomes. This discipline promotes fiscally smart decisions about when and how to use AI capabilities and can drive a top-down culture change.

“The same tokens can go to a skilled engineer shipping a product faster, or to a non-expert generating 10 versions of the same slide deck,” says Tom Shea, CEO and cofounder at OneStream. “The line item in the budget looks identical either way, and true token efficacy requires governance to ensure those tokens are empowering experts to accelerate output, rather than fueling a massive cost explosion.”

Recommendation: Setting AI budgets too soon may curtail employees’ enthusiasm in learning and experimenting with AI. Establish financial targets based on a maturity curve to encourage experimentation first, then fiscal discipline when AI agents are deployed to production.

CIOs should communicate these two cost considerations to DevOps teams using AI code generators.

First, according to Stack Overflow’s 2026 Developer Survey, 73% of developers use AI coding assistants and agents daily, but developers care more about quality (75%) over cost (38%) when shaping prompts and picking models. CIOs should set guidelines for balancing cost and quality tradeoffs, establish DevOps non-negotiables, and require code analysis in deployment pipelines.

“Coding is no longer a constraint, and the bottleneck has moved to how we ensure the correctness of code,” says Anurag Dhingra, SVP and GM of networking and collaboration at Cisco. “There’s just no humanly possible way to review every piece of code that is written by AI.”

The problem is that 96% of developers don’t fully trust AI-generated code and 48% always check their AI-assisted code before committing, according to Sonar’s State of Code Developer Survey. As large organizations may use several AI code-generating tools, they need to benchmark quality, cost, and developer satisfaction.

“Teams need clear guardrails and engineering standards, especially as AI agents accelerate development and can introduce costly rework,” says Andrea Malagodi, CTO at Sonar. “Having live data aggregated from your one or many providers, to enable you to see the cost per PR [pull request], is a good governance mechanism.”

Recommendation: While AI code generation is a remarkable breakthrough, it also brings new costs and quality considerations CIOs should track.

Another cost consideration comes as organizations deploy hundreds of AI agents and provide developers several AI models to choose from. Developers may choose models based on preferences rather than performance and cost considerations.

Craig Wiley, VP of AI at Databricks, says 77% of companies now juggle multiple model families because the best model for one task is rarely the best for another. “The flexibility comes at a cost of managing shifting prices, scattered vendors, and zero visibility into where your budget’s actually going. The fix is real-time budgets and smart routing that automatically sends queries to the most cost-effective model,” Wiley says.

cim: Így szaladhat meg a vállalati AI-költségvetés
lead: A nem mért kísérletezés, a hiányzó szabályozás és a drága modellek túlzott használata gyorsan felemésztheti az AI-projektekre szánt keretet.
osszefoglalo:
Az AI-kísérletezésről a mindennapi működésre való áttérés során sok cég szembesül a gyorsan növekvő **AI-adóssággal és váratlan költségekkel**. A szakértői tapasztalatok szerint a leggyakoribb hiba a konkrét üzleti célok hiánya, aminek következtében a tesztelések és a tesztüzemben ragadt AI-ügynökök érdemi eredmény nélkül égetik a büdzsét.

A túlköltekezést a hiányos **irányítási szabályzatok** és a gyenge adatalapok is tetézik. Sok esetben a fejlesztők és munkatársak megszokásból a legdrágább modellt használják olyan feladatokra is, amelyeket olcsóbb, célzott modellekkel vagy automatizációkkal is el lehetne végezni.

A költségek kézben tartásához elengedhetetlen a központi platformok használata, az intelligens modellirányítás és a folyamatos adatminőség-ellenőrzés.
miert_szamit: A kísérletezés szakaszából továbblépve **minden AI-ügynökhöz és automatizációhoz mérhető üzleti célt** és költségkeretet kell rendelni a fenntartható működés érdekében.

prioritas.lead_hu: Sok vállalat elhamarkodottan vásárol MI-licenceket, ami jelentős pluszköltségekhez és biztonsági kockázatokhoz vezet. A CIO-k az új technológia bevezetésénél a korábbi informatikai hibákat ismétlik meg.

tenyellenorzes.esemeny: A CIO magazin cikkében szakértők foglalják össze, milyen hibák miatt szaladhat meg a vállalatok AI-költségvetése a kísérletezésről a termelésbe való átállás során.
